newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian PM says World Bank made wrong decision.
newsitem.headline: Croatian PM says World Bank made wrong decision.

text.p: Croatian Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa on Wednesday criticised a World Bank decision to delay a $30 million loan to Croatia, made after a request from the United States, as "a totally wrong policy".
Matesa said he believed the World Bank was being used for political means.
"To be very honest, I think that it is a totally wrong policy," he told Reuters at an international conference on transition economies.

"We are talking about a loan. It is something which by definition has to be paid back. It is not a gift and I do not think the World Bank is an institution which (should) be used for political means," Matesa said.
Asked if he believed the bank was being used for political means, Matesa answered: "Absolutely".

A U.S. official said on Monday that Washington was asking the World Bank to postpone the release of the loan because Zagreb had not followed through on its commitments, including extraditing suspected war criminals made under the Dayton peace accord.
Zagreb has come under pressure from Washington in the past few weeks to make progress on promises made when it signed the treaty which ended the 4-1/2 year war in former Yugoslavia in November 1995.
A World Bank press officer said in Washington on Tuesday the discussion on the Croatian loan had been postponed at the request of the international organisation's U.S. executive director.
She said the talks "may be taken up at the next board meeting, but we do not have a date yet".
U.S. State Department spokesman John Dinger said the current delay was for two days, but the United States hoped for a longer postponement and was seeking support for this from its allies.

Dinger said Washington wanted the loan debate delayed while it monitors progress in three areas of concern -- Croatia's use of its influence in bringing war criminals to justice, the need for concrete progress on the return of Serb refugees and other displaced persons and the need for more border crossings with Bosnia.

"We believe that Croatia's lack of cooperation on Dayton undermines prospects for regional stability and also calls into question Croatia's commitment to implement and sustain economic programmes that are necessary for prosperity," Dinger said.
